children: The energy transition is reshaping workforce needs, making interdisciplinary skills, continuous learning and talent development central to the sector’s future

India’s power sector is undergoing a significant transformation, driven by the evolution of electricity markets, increasing renewable energy integration and the adoption of digital technologies. These developments are reshaping how electricity is generated, traded and consumed, while changing the skills and competencies required across the sector.

As power markets become more sophisticated, professionals need specialised domain knowledge, analytical capabilities and technological proficiency. However, finding individuals who understand electricity markets and possess the necessary technical and commercial expertise remains a challenge.

One reason is the traditional separation of academic and professional disciplines. Engineering, finance, economics and technology have largely evolved as distinct streams of education and employment. Modern power markets, however, require professionals who can understand how these disciplines interact and influence one another.
Power Markets Require Multidisciplinary Skills

The evolution of India's electricity markets has expanded the range of professional competencies required across the sector. The development of organised electricity trading mechanisms, including the Day Ahead Market, Term Ahead Market, Real Time Market and Green Day Ahead Market, has increased the complexity of electricity procurement and trading.

Market participants must navigate changing demand patterns, generation availability, price movements and regulatory provisions, often within shorter decision-making cycles. This requires an understanding of how market mechanisms operate and how operational, commercial and regulatory factors influence trading decisions.

The sector therefore needs professionals who can combine knowledge of power systems with an understanding of market economics, data analytics, financial fundamentals and regulatory frameworks. The ability to interpret market information, identify emerging trends and assess the commercial implications of operational decisions is becoming increasingly important.
Energy Transition Redefines Workforce Needs

The integration of renewable energy is expanding the range of skills required across the power sector. Forecasting, scheduling, balancing and storage management are becoming important areas of expertise as solar and wind generation account for a growing share of electricity supply. Battery storage and hybrid renewable projects will further increase the need for professionals who understand both their technical and commercial aspects.

The employment implications are considerable. Recent studies estimate that India’s clean energy ambitions could generate over 50 lakh employment opportunities, with a substantial proportion of jobs in clean energy project deployment requiring semi-skilled and highly skilled workers. This points to the need for workforce development to keep pace with the sector’s expansion.

The changing composition of these jobs is also significant. Alongside conventional engineering and project management roles, the sector will increasingly require professionals specialising in energy forecasting, market operations, data science, regulatory affairs and digital infrastructure.

Meeting these requirements will involve drawing on skills from different professional backgrounds. Experience in financial services, information technology and data analytics can provide relevant capabilities for emerging roles in the power sector. However, professionals moving into these roles will also need sector-specific knowledge to apply their existing expertise effectively within the electricity market ecosystem.
Bridging The Classroom-Workplace Gap

A graduate entering the power sector may have studied electrical systems, economics or computer science in considerable depth without having examined an electricity trading platform or worked with actual market data. Theoretical foundations remain essential, but limited exposure to industry applications can make the transition into specialised roles difficult.

Academic curricula need greater flexibility to address this gap. An electrical engineering student interested in power markets could benefit from courses in economics and data analytics, while a computer science graduate could develop foundational knowledge of electricity markets. Such interdisciplinary learning could widen the pool of suitable candidates without requiring every professional to pursue an entirely new academic pathway.

Closer engagement between educational institutions and industry can also help students understand how theoretical concepts translate into workplace responsibilities. Practical exposure to market operations, regulatory frameworks and data-driven decision-making can make graduates better prepared for specialised roles.
HR Must Anticipate Future Skills

Recruitment alone cannot address the changing requirements of the power sector. Organisations need to assess how existing roles are evolving and identify the capabilities employees are likely to require over the next three to five years.

Artificial intelligence and advanced analytics add another dimension to workforce planning. Their applications in demand forecasting, predictive analytics, automated decision support and operational efficiency are likely to influence several power sector functions. Employees will need to work with these tools, interpret their outputs and apply sound domain judgement when making decisions. Although technology may automate certain processes, contextual understanding and informed judgement will remain important.

Candidate assessment also needs to account for changing skill requirements. Recruitment frameworks that place excessive weight on conventional qualifications may overlook individuals with relevant analytical, technological or commercial capabilities. Evaluating domain knowledge alongside problem-solving ability and a willingness to learn can provide a broader assessment of a candidate’s potential.

Continuous learning will be equally important. Structured training, cross-functional exposure, mentoring and opportunities to work on emerging business challenges can help employees broaden their capabilities and prepare for changing responsibilities. These efforts can also help organisations develop existing talent instead of relying exclusively on external recruitment to fill specialised roles.
Building The Talent Foundation

India's power markets are entering a phase in which institutional development, technological advancement and workforce capabilities need to progress together. The evolution of electricity exchanges, increasing renewable energy integration and the growing use of digital technologies will continue to reshape the skills required across the sector.

Developing this workforce will require coordinated efforts from industry participants, educational institutions, policymakers and professional bodies. Academic institutions will need to create more opportunities for interdisciplinary learning, while employers will need to invest in continuous capability development and provide greater exposure to real-world applications.

Aligning education, recruitment and professional development with the changing requirements of power markets will be essential to building a workforce capable of responding to the sector’s evolving technical, commercial and regulatory demands.
Brijesh Narang
Guest Author The author is the Vice President – Human Resources at Indian Energy Exchange (IEX).
